Hub star: the same old bus

Over time the topology went from bus to star: a concentrator, the hub, with the stations connected to it.

The hub is a physical layer device, a repeater: it receives the signal on one port, regenerates it and copies it to all the other ports. It behaves exactly like a bus.

If ports run out, another hub is added with a crossover cable, and the bus gets bigger: all the stations form a single collision domain and compete for the only 10 Mbps.
The shape of the cabling changed, not how it works: it is still CSMA/CD over a shared medium.
Two stations and a crossover cable: full-duplex

We want to connect two stations directly. A regular cable doesn't work: both interfaces are electrically identical.

The crossover cable swaps the pins: one station's transmit pin reaches the other's receive pin. This gives two independent channels.

It no longer makes sense to listen to the medium or look for collisions, because they can't occur. We go from half-duplex to full-duplex and drop CSMA/CD: 10 Mbps from A to B and 10 Mbps from B to A.
With no shared medium there are no collisions, pauses or wasted time: bandwidth is doubled.
Point-to-point link: each direction travels over its own pair, so the two frames cross without interfering.

The network grows: more hubs, more stations, and all of them still share the same 10 Mbps. Performance drops.

To improve it, a bridge is used. It is plugged into the network and operates transparently: to the stations it doesn't exist.

The bridge splits the medium into segments, and each one is a separate collision domain. Now each pair of stations shares the 10 Mbps of its segment.
Fewer stations competing for each segment = fewer collisions and better performance.
A sends to B and D sends to C at the same time. They don't collide: each transmission stays in its own segment.

Once connected, the bridge learns the MAC addresses to know which side each station is on. It stores them in an internal table of limited size (this determines the extent of the network).

With the table it decides whether the frame crosses or not:

  • Sender and recipient on the same segment: it filters it.
  • Recipient on the other segment: it lets it through.

It always lets broadcast frames through.
The bridge separates collision domains, but it doesn't stop broadcasts.
To cross, the bridge is just another station

When the recipient is on the other side, the bridge works just like a station:

  • A listens to its segment and transmits.
  • The bridge receives the frame and stores it in a buffer.
  • Then it listens to the other segment and, when it is free, transmits it.

In other words, the bridge shares the 10 Mbps with the stations on the first segment and with those on the second, separately.
The bridge does CSMA/CD on each segment: a collision on one side never propagates to the other.
A segment with a single station

We add one more port to the bridge and on that segment we connect a single station, X. It is loaded into the table like the others.

X competes with nobody for the resource: it has the whole segment to itself and is connected directly to the bridge. So it can enable the full-duplex interface and transmit and receive at the same time: 10 Mbps each way.

The other two segments remain shared, with CSMA/CD.
A station alone on its port doesn't need CSMA/CD. The switch is born from this observation.
Switch: a bridge with many ports

Let's take the idea to the extreme: the switch is a bridge with many more ports, so that all stations connect to it, each in full-duplex mode.

The hub is a physical layer repeater; the switch works at the data link layer: it knows who is on each port, it knows their MAC addresses.

It is still transparent: the stations don't know it's there. If a frame arrives for an address that isn't in the table, it copies it to all ports.
Each station has its own link: two different conversations happen at once without bothering each other.

What if two stations send to the same one at the same time? They don't collide:

  • Each frame is stored in the buffer of the port it came in on.
  • From there it is copied to the destination MAC port.
  • When the switch can, it transmits it to the station.

The sending station thinks it has already delivered the message, but in reality it was stored in the switch.

If a port has a hub on it, there the switch waits for the medium to be free using CSMA/CD and collisions can occur.
In the switch, frames wait their turn in a buffer; they no longer destroy each other.

To switch a frame, the switch needs the destination MAC, which comes in the first field of the frame.

  • Cut-through: it decides as soon as it receives those 6 bytes. With hubs, 58 bytes remain inside the collision window: the already-switched frame may end up truncated.
  • Fragment-free: it waits for the first 64 bytes, which cover the collision window.
  • Store-and-forward: it waits for the full frame, checks the CRC and, if it is correct, switches it.
The longer the switch waits, the slower it switches and the fewer damaged frames it forwards.

Highlighted: what the switch has to receive before deciding. Cut-through is the fastest but may forward truncated frames; store-and-forward is the slowest and the only one that verifies the CRC; fragment-free is the middle ground.
From hub to switch at a glance

• Hub: physical layer repeater. A single collision domain, 10 Mbps for everyone.
  • Full-duplex: with a point-to-point link there are no collisions and CSMA/CD is unnecessary.
  • Bridge: splits collision domains, learns MACs, filters or forwards. Lets broadcasts through.
  • Switch: bridge with many ports, buffers and full-duplex.
  • Modes: cut-through (6 bytes), fragment-free (64) and store-and-forward (full frame).

Bridges are transparent and don't know about each other. In the next lesson we see the problem this causes when there are redundant paths: loops, and how Spanning Tree solves them.

A bridge receives a frame whose sender and recipient are on the same segment. What does it do?
Filters it: doesn't pass it to the other segment
Sends it back to the sender
With its MAC table it knows both are on the same side; it only lets the frame through when the recipient is on another segment (and always broadcasts).
Why can a station connected alone to a bridge or switch port use full-duplex?
Because the switch gives it higher priority
Because it shares the segment with nobody: there can be no collisions
Because it uses a shorter preamble
Because the switch is a physical layer device
Since it doesn't compete with other stations for the medium, CSMA/CD isn't needed and it can transmit and receive at once.
Which switching mode waits for the first 64 bytes before forwarding?
Fragment-free waits for the collision window (64 bytes) so as not to switch a frame that ends up truncated; cut-through waits for 6 bytes and store-and-forward for the full frame.

Set of stations that compete for the same medium (the same 10 Mbps) and can collide with each other.

Transparent. Splits collision domains, learns MACs in a table, filters or forwards. Broadcasts always pass.

Data link layer bridge with many ports: one station per port, full-duplex, buffers, no collisions. Unknown destination → copies to all.
